i think this is difficult conceptually since configuring a systemd target loses all information about what that target is intended to do.

If the pre- and post-condition is hardcoded in the device-specific firmware update daemon then the potential for misconfiguration is removed.

Since the pre- and post-condition is device specific.

Can you provide any specific example of a use-case for the pre- and post-update target that can or should not be solved inside the device-specific update daemon.

> i think this is difficult conceptually since configuring a systemd target loses all information about what that target is intended to do.

Not sure what you mean by "configuring a systemd target loses all information about what that target is intended to do."?
> 
> If the pre- and post-condition is hardcoded in the device-specific firmware update daemon then the potential for misconfiguration is removed.

Not all Code Updater deamons are device specific. PLDMd is one such example which can handle update for wide variety of PLDM devices, which can have different pre and post conditions. Also, for same device type pre and post conditions can change depending upon the platform type and where that particular component is positioned.

> 
> Since the pre- and post-condition is device specific.

pre and post systemd targets can be device specific too.

> 
> Can you provide any specific example of a use-case for the pre- and post-update target that can or should not be solved inside the device-specific update daemon.

As i mentioned above, PLDMd is such an example which handles update for all PLDM devices and pre & post conditions for devices can be different depending upon the platform type.

It's important to understand that not all CodeUpdater daemons need to implement this extension. If the CodeUpdater daemon can benefit from using it and it provides some abstraction, then it can choose to do so. That's why the wording says "the Code Updater daemon can be configured" rather than "the Code Updater daemon should be configured". For example, if we think it doesn't make much sense to add this extension for flash-based updates of BIOS, we can always skip it since it's all internal workings.

Keep in mind that these conditions can be very hardware or platform specific and can involve all sorts of arbitrary operations.

> how to expect to specifcy pre post conditions in EM

Just list the different pre- and post-conditions. Providing a way to put any arbitrary systemd service is destabilizing the whole thing. In this entire discussion there was never once an specific example of any such condition.

It usually goes like this
- provide extension point for flexibility
- extension point becomes widely used, people assume it is required
- depending on device, extension point is now required to work, people avoid patching the code updater since it's easier to just write systemd service in their own layer
- extension point implicitly becomes required part of the design
- the default (without extension point) does not work anymore

There are many examples of this
- the ipmi UUID thingy (need custom dbus service to make 'ipmitool mc guid' work)
- phosphor-watchdog
- bmcweb redfish event log (needs rsyslog to be configured separately to make it work)

> Keep in mind that these conditions can be very hardware or platform specific and can involve all sorts of arbitrary operations.

When the code updater is done updating the device, the update is complete.
If there is any steps needed as part of the update process, the code updater is responsible for completing those steps.

When the code updater is done, anything after that is not part of the update process. So there is no need for the code updater to start any service, since the update is already complete.

I am not sure how the examples you mentioned are applicable to the patch in question.
But as part of my latest change, i have updated the description to reflect that is not for every kind of daemon and daemon can choose to not use it if doesn't map to its functioning or implementation. But certain daemon would have this use case, such as PLDM so its being added for such.

> I am not sure how the examples you mentioned are applicable to the patch in question.

The examples work via extension points which are unnecessary for the daemons involved, for the specific thing that they do.

You cannot code each and every hardware's detail and way of working into the common code, thats why abstractions are developed. And i have already given PLDMd as a concrete example which can do dyanamic discovery of connected devices and use standard PLDM spec to update the devices (common code). Now some device specific actions such as device reset (lets say via some gpio) after update can be performed in these hooks.

If so, why is it not part of a configuration for a device?

> Sorry for the dumb question, but which configuration file?

The platform can offer a configuration file in a specific format, such as JSON, which is commonly used by various daemons in openBMC.

> 
> Will it be part of EM configuration? 

No, it's not part of the EM configuration because I received feedback in the past to avoid specifying systemd targets in the EM configuration. However, it can be included in daemon-specific configurations.

> 
> If so, why is it not part of a configuration for a device?

For the reason I previously stated.

> Instead of having all of this as a separate ```Components``` array it
> could be configured in the json object for the specific device.
> 
> That would make it easier for a code updater daemon to extract the config.
> 
> If it should not be part of EM config, why not?

Yes, it would have been straightforward to include this in the EM configuration since the previous patch already defined it for updatable components. However, there is a reason why it cannot be added, as I mentioned earlier.

> No, it's not part of the EM configuration because I received feedback in the past to avoid specifying systemd targets in the EM configuration. However, it can be included in daemon-specific configurations.

I believe we should be preferring EM based configuration since that it can be probed on specific devices and dbus interfaces.

With the daemon specific configuration it is problematic since it is fixed.
So the configuration already has to include all the components which may or may not be there which creates overhead and favors a fixed chassis configuration.

Also it will not be intuitive for users that they have to configure the Code Updater daemon both with EM config and also with the daemon specific configuration.

Then there is the additional implementation overhead of detecting mismatch between those 2 configurations. Since they are inherently mismatched (dynamic vs static configuration)

> > No, it's not part of the EM configuration because I received feedback in the past to avoid specifying systemd targets in the EM configuration. However, it can be included in daemon-specific configurations.
> 
> I believe we should be preferring EM based configuration since that it can be probed on specific devices and dbus interfaces.
> 
> With the daemon specific configuration it is problematic since it is fixed.

Don't understand what you mean by fixed?

> So the configuration already has to include all the components which may or may not be there which creates overhead and favors a fixed chassis configuration.

It seems that you are under the impression that there is only one version of the configuration file for all platforms and devices. However, this is not the case. Each platform can specify its own overrides in the openbmc/openbmc repo within its meta layer. These overrides are specified using .bbappend files on the original recipe and are installed in a location in the filesystem as expected by the daemon. For example, in the case of PLDMd, platformX will specify this configuration file in the openbmc/openbmc repo depending upon the devices that can be discovered dynamically on that platform.

> 
> Also it will not be intuitive for users that they have to configure the Code Updater daemon both with EM config and also with the daemon specific configuration.
> 
> Then there is the additional implementation overhead of detecting mismatch between those 2 configurations. Since they are inherently mismatched (dynamic vs static configuration)

I think it will be worth to understand why systemd targets are not preferred in EM configuration. I share the same concern that we have to configure both EM and daemon specific configuration which makes platform portability harder.

The pre and post update services are optional and every component updater is not suppose to have them. The CodeUpdater will try to discover these services via GetUnitFileState. If they exist, CodeUpdater will execute them, otherwise it will log a warning message saying the service doesn't exist. This warning message can be used by the developer to perform any debugging in their development environments. I have added these details to the doc.

GetUnitFileState to know if a service exists and StartUnit/JobRemoved to watch the lifetime of pre and post service. * What is that code updater doesn't know about*

Warning is misleading if GetUnitFileState says a service doesn't exist, if there are failures in starting/completion then it is acceptable.

How will be the RF update task be updated if the pre or post service fails?

> >there is no response from the code updater

> What is that code updater has to respond for in this case?

My understanding of what @alexander.hansen@9elements.com meant by this is if the CodeUpdater doesn't execute the pre/post service even though the service has specified and packaged it, so some signal is needed in that case to show the service didn't run.

> 
> >unclear if the code updater knows about the service.
> GetUnitFileState to know if a service exists and StartUnit/JobRemoved to watch the lifetime of pre and post service. * What is that code updater doesn't know about*
> 
> Warning is misleading if GetUnitFileState says a service doesn't exist, if there are failures in starting/completion then it is acceptable.

CodeUpdater has no info if the service exists or not, as its discovered at runtime using GetUnitFileState (ServiceName created implicitly using `Device Name`), a signal is given to the user if the service is not found, which is using this warning message. The failure is an error condition, which would actually fail the update.

> 
> How will be the RF update task be updated if the pre or post service fails?

If Pre/Post condition exists, then for ApplyTime == Immediate, any failure in Pre/Post will cause ActivationStatus failure which accordingly update the RF state. For ApplyTime == OnReset, only pre condition applies and any failure in that will mark the ActivationStatus as failed, which accordingly update the RF state.
On how ActivationStatus gets handled in BMCWeb, you can refer to UpdateService in BMCWeb.

The hierarchy looks fine. Device -> Components. It works for me.

My feedback is regarding the Identifier for Device & Components. In the implementation for CodeUpdater irrespective of whether it is PLDM or Non-PLDM, the CodeUpdater knows the device and components it is updating. The CodeUpdater needs to know which is the "Identifier" to look in the configuration to see whether something applicable for itself. 

My suggestion is that the "Identifier" for devices and components should match to how it modelled on OpenBMC. So a *Device* is modelled as D-Bus object in the /xyz/openbmc_project/chassis namespace implementing inventory interfaces and *Component* is modelled as D-Bus object in xyz/openbmc_project/software namespace implementing the SW.Version interface. Since the CodeUpdater is aware of the device and respective components it is updating, it can look up the configuration based on that.
